claims.text: The starting Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase and chemically homogeneous.
Heating rate governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid heating limits diffusion-mediated atomic rearrangement and preserves a disordered atomic configuration.
The rapidly preserved disordered configuration has high mixing entropy.
Preserving high mixing entropy raises the effective melting point of the nanoparticles.
Rapid heating produces a sharper, more discrete melting transition.
Slow heating permits local atomic rearrangement and ordering.
Locally ordered clusters act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Formation of locally ordered clusters lowers the onset temperature of premelting.
The controlled comparison uses rapid pulsed-laser heating versus conventional slow furnace heating on otherwise identical nanoparticle batches.
The rapid and slow heating rates are approximately 10^3 K/s and 10 K/min, respectively, while maximum temperature, atmosphere, and temperature uniformity are controlled.
Rapidly heated particles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than slow-heated baseline particles.
Rapidly heated particles will have a sharper melting transition than slow-heated baseline particles.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles in a typical size range represented by approximately 60 nm particles.
Excessive thermal gradients, other size-dependent effects, or significant external perturbations may invalidate the mechanism.
The magnitude of the temperature shift and degree of ordering may vary with particle size and experimental conditions.
A controlled absence of significant differences in premelting onset and melting-transition sharpness between rapid and slow heating would falsify the proposed kinetic-ordering mechanism.
